title: Democrats Capture Both Houses of Congress in Midterm Rebuke of Trump
excerpt: Democrats flipped six Republican Senate seats, including Texas for the first time since 1988, while Indian-American candidates won in Virginia, Maryland and Florida and Vivek Ramaswamy lost in Ohio.
body:
• Democrats have captured both the House and the Senate, according to projections by Decision Desk HQ and NBC News, ending Republican control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.
  • Democrats flipped Senate seats in Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa — more than the net gain of four they needed — including the first Democratic Senate win in Texas since 1988.
  • Indian-American Democrats Suhas Subramanyam, Aruna Miller and Pia Dandiya won their races, while Republican Vivek Ramaswamy lost the Ohio governor's race to Democrat Amy Acton, the Associated Press reported.
  • For Indian Americans, a Democratic Congress changes the politics of immigration, H-1B visas and trade with India: the new majority has pledged to reverse Medicaid and food-stamp cuts and to reassert Congress's role on trade policy.

Democrats have won control of both chambers of Congress, pushing deep into traditionally Republican territory to flip states and districts President Donald Trump carried, according to projections by Decision Desk HQ and NBC News reported by USA Today. The House majority was projected earlier in the evening; the Senate call followed as Democrats flipped a string of Republican-held seats.

"In Texas, Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the state since 1988."

A Senate map that broke the wrong way for Republicans

Democrats flipped Senate seats in South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa, USA Today reported — comfortably more than the net gain of four they needed to take the chamber, after entering election night needing to flip at least three seats in states Trump won in 2024. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the state since 1988. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton was projected to be the first Democrat to win a Senate seat since 1932. A competitive Michigan race, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to hold the seat for his party, remained uncalled.

USA Today reported that Trump's dipping popularity and the rising cost of living reshaped the midterm outlook, and that Democrats campaigned relentlessly on the White House's failure to tame the economy while pressing allegations of corruption against the president and his allies.

Indian-American winners — and a high-profile loss in Ohio

It was a strong night for Indian-American Democrats in the races The Videshi tracked on election day. Congressman Suhas Subramanyam was re-elected in Virginia's 10th Congressional District, taking about 63 percent of the vote to Republican Dave Beckwith's 35 percent with roughly 82 percent of ballots counted, according to NBC News figures reported by IANS. In Maryland, Lieutenant Governor Aruna Miller won another term as Governor Wes Moore defeated Republican Dan Cox. And in Florida's 22nd Congressional District, educator Pia Dandiya defeated Republican Casey Askar, according to a CBS News projection reported by IANS.

The community's most prominent Republican candidate fell short. In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy in the governor's race, according to the Associated Press, which called the race at 10:49 p.m. Eastern. With about 88 percent of precincts reporting, Acton had 2,136,587 votes to Ramaswamy's 1,913,613. Acton, who served as Ohio's health director under outgoing Republican Governor Mike DeWine, becomes the first woman elected governor of Ohio and the first Democrat to win the office in 20 years. The closing weeks of the race were dominated by a controversial Ramaswamy campaign advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother.

In Arizona's 1st Congressional District, Democrat Amish Shah, an emergency-room doctor, led Republican Jay Feely with 136,277 votes to 107,247 in Associated Press tabulations with about 70 percent of precincts reporting; the race was still too early to call.

What a Democratic Congress means

Retaking the Senate gives Democrats leverage over Washington's agenda for the rest of Trump's term. USA Today reported the party is likely to pursue reversing Medicaid and food-stamp cuts, reasserting Congress's role on foreign trade policy, and seeking bipartisan agreement on banning lawmakers from trading stocks. Trump will also face a harder path confirming Cabinet and judicial nominees, including for any Supreme Court vacancy. The most immediate confrontation, USA Today reported, is likely to center on the war in Iran, where Democrats could press the president to seek congressional authorization to continue the conflict or move to pull its funding.

For the diaspora, the practical stakes run through immigration and trade: committees that oversee visa policy, and a Congress reasserting itself on tariffs, will both be chaired by Democrats for the next two years. Several Indian-American races — including contests in New York, California and Los Angeles — were still being counted as this article was published and will be covered as they are called.
